object.medium: Piece for solo piano, third movement of the Suite bergamasque; engraved first edition
object.description: Debussy sketched the four pieces of his Suite bergamasque around 1890, when he was twenty-eight and almost unknown, but he put them aside. Fifteen years later, now famous for Pelléas et Mélisande and La mer, he was persuaded by the publisher Fromont to revise and release them, and the suite appeared in Paris in 1905. The third piece, originally called 'Promenade sentimentale', was renamed 'Clair de lune' after a poem by Paul Verlaine in which masked revellers sing 'in the calm moonlight, sad and beautiful'. Its hushed opening in D-flat major, with chords that float rather than progress, became the best-known example of the new harmonic language later called impressionist, and one of the most loved piano pieces ever written. The page shown is the first page of the 1905 Fromont edition. The visitor hears the piece played by the Dutch pianist Laurens Goedhart, who released his 2011 recording under a Creative Commons Attribution licence.
facts: The title comes from Verlaine's poem 'Clair de lune' in Fêtes galantes (1869), which Debussy also set twice as a song.
The word 'bergamasque' refers to a rustic dance from Bergamo mentioned in the same poem.
Debussy never recorded the piece; his few piano rolls, made in 1913, are of other works.
